name: Cinderblock Nightwatch Wrap Set
description: Built for low-visibility, low-movement work — the kind of watching that happens in doorways and on broken catwalks at 03:00. The foundation is a thermal long-sleeve base in charcoal heather, heavily pilled from repeated washing in whatever water is available, the neck stretched wide and re-hemmed with a doubled strip of elastic salvaged from a Pragma Systems base layer. Over this is a structured wrap-jacket in a deep, muted rust-brown — originally a single-piece garment, now split at the left side seam and re-closed with a row of mismatched pressure snaps that allow rapid removal or ventilation adjustment. The wrap folds across the chest and ties with a wide obi-style sash in faded indigo, its ends frayed to loose threads that the wearer has stopped cutting. The sash carries two flat pockets stitched directly onto it — one holding a folded emergency mylar sheet, one with a broken-seam closure holding a small medkit. The lower half is loose trousers in near-black canvas, hem-gathered at the ankle with salvaged elastic so they don't snag on debris, the left thigh bearing a large iron-on acid-shield patch in matte gray. Footwear is a low boot in cracked synthetic suede, the toe cap reinforced with a strip of steel salvaged from a junction box cover, riveted in place with hardware-store bolts. The head covering is a wide, flat-crown wrap cap in washed linen the color of old concrete, its brim stiffened with a strip of reclaimed wire sewn into the hem. The whole palette — rust, indigo shadow, charcoal, near-black — is dark enough to disappear in Shelf shadows but not so uniform as to read as tactical.
functionality: Wrap-jacket with snap-release side for rapid removal; sash-mounted flat pockets; ankle-gathered trousers prevent debris snagging; reinforced steel toe cap; wire-stiffened brim cap for weather and concealment; muted palette for low-visibility work
what_it_says: This is community infrastructure clothing — the person who wears this is probably keeping watch over something or someone. The obi sash signals a hand-craft tradition maintained even under Shelf conditions, a quiet insistence on form. The mismatched snaps and frayed threads say the form comes second to function, but not by much. There's dignity here, worn thin but intact.
worn_by: runners who move between Shelf districts after dark
elders who remember when the obi meant something specific
manufacturer: Self-assembled; wrap fabric sourced from a collapsed textile market stall; sash is repurposed Tier 2 import fabric
price_range: Φ 18–40 complete; Φ 5–12 for sash alone on secondary market
story_hooks: The indigo sash is cut from a garment that belonged to someone who didn't survive the last major Shelf flooding — the wearer knows this and so does anyone from that neighborhood who sees it.
The flat pocket on the sash contains something besides a medkit: a folded document, handwritten, that someone paid to have delivered and the wearer hasn't decided whether to deliver it yet.

A TESSERA field agent doing gene-mod compliance sweeps stops the wearer specifically because the ankle-gathered trousers are a known style marker for people running unlicensed geneware underground — it's a profiling assumption, and it may or may not be correct.
